sections.heading: Where St. Clair Shores crashes happen

c.v: The I-94 interchanges and service drives.
I-94 carries commuter traffic to Detroit and through traffic to Port Huron, with interchanges and service drives at the mile roads only a mile apart. The crashes are:

items.v: rear-end crashes in the stop-and-go, and where traffic backs up from the exit ramps onto the freeway
merge and weave crashes between closely spaced entrance and exit ramps
crashes at the ramp terminals and service-drive signals, where drivers turn across the service drive onto the mile road
left-turn crashes at the mile-road signals just east of the freeway

c.v: In the State Police’s 2025 intersection data, 12 Mile at I-94 had 86 crashes, third in Macomb County, and 10 Mile at I-94 had 66, ninth. The freeway and its ramps belong to MDOT. See our
St. Clair Shores truck accident page
Jefferson Avenue and the Nautical Mile.

Jefferson runs along the lake from the Grosse Pointe line to the Harrison Township line. Between about Nine and Ten Mile, the Nautical Mile adds marinas, boat dealers, waterfront restaurants, and bars, and the city’s lakefront parks draw summer crowds. The crashes are:

items.v: drunk-driving crashes leaving the restaurants and bars, often late at night
pedestrians struck crossing Jefferson between the parking lots and the restaurants
cars and trucks towing boat trailers, turning into and out of the marinas and the launches
left turns into restaurant and marina driveways across oncoming traffic (MCL 257.650)
cyclists on Jefferson, struck by passing or turning drivers

Harper Avenue.
The city’s inland commercial strip, with stores, restaurants, and dozens of driveways between the mile roads. The crashes are:

items.v: left-turn and red-light crashes at the mile-road signals
driveway crashes, where a driver leaving a lot must yield to traffic on the road (MCL 257.652)
rear-end crashes at the signals and behind turning cars
pedestrians struck near the stores and bus stops

c.v: Greater Mack, Little Mack, and the mile roads.

Greater Mack runs past homes and schools between Harper and Jefferson, and Little Mack runs along the freeway. The mile roads cross the city from I-94 to the lake. The crashes are intersection crashes at the signals and four-way stops, school-zone crashes, and drivers pulling out from side streets.
Whose road it is: the State, the county, or the City.
St. Clair Shores is a city, and road ownership is split:
MDOT

items.v: owns I-94 and its ramps. A road-defect claim against MDOT goes to the Court of Claims, with written notice filed there within 120 days (MCL 691.1404).

c.v: Macomb County

items.v: (the Department of Roads) or the City of St. Clair Shores owns Jefferson, Harper, Greater Mack, Little Mack, and the mile roads, depending on the segment. The I-94 service drives may belong to MDOT or to the local agency, depending on the stretch.

c.v: The City

items.v: owns the local streets.

c.v: The State Police recorded no crashes on U.S. or state routes in the city in 2024. Apart from I-94, the major roads are county or City roads.

A claim against the county or the City requires written notice within 120 days (MCL 691.1402, 691.1404). A pothole or other defect in the road can make the agency a defendant alongside the other driver; on State and county roads, signals, signs, and sight obstructions generally fall outside the highway exception (Nawrocki v Macomb County Road Commission, Mich 2000). The notice must go to the agency that actually has jurisdiction over that stretch of road, or it is no notice.

In a rear-end crash, fault is rarely disputed. At an I-94 merge, a service-drive signal, a Harper driveway, or a Jefferson crossing, it often is, and the other driver’s insurer may try to assign you half or more of the fault. That share matters (MCL 500.3135(2)(b)):
More than 50 percent at fault:

items.v: you lose your claim for pain and suffering.

c.v: 50 percent or less:

items.v: your recovery is reduced by your share. At exactly 50 percent, you recover half.

sections.heading: When the other driver was drunk: the claim against the bar

c.v: A bar, restaurant, or store that serves alcohol to a visibly intoxicated person, or to a minor, is liable for the injuries that person causes under Michigan’s dram shop act (MCL 436.1801). After a crash involving a driver leaving the Nautical Mile or a Harper bar, that claim can matter more than the claim against the driver:
The drunk driver’s own policy is often small,

items.v: or the driver has none. The bar’s liquor liability policy is a separate source of payment.

c.v: The evidence is the bar’s,

items.v: and it does not last: point-of-sale receipts, tabs, cameras, staff schedules, and the witnesses who saw the driver served.

c.v: The claim has its own rules.

items.v: Written notice must go to the business within 120 days after you hire a lawyer. The drunk driver must be named and kept in the suit. The suit must be filed within two years, not three.

c.v: The police report, the driver’s blood alcohol result, and the timeline from receipts usually show where the driver was drinking. A driver may have been served at more than one place.

A rideshare ride home is often how people leave the Nautical Mile. A passenger or another driver hurt in a crash with a rideshare vehicle may have a claim against the rideshare company’s commercial policy, which applies during a trip and often has higher limits than a personal policy. See our

sections.heading: Who pays after a St. Clair Shores crash

c.v: Your no-fault (PIP) claim.
Your own auto insurer pays these benefits regardless of fault (MCL 500.3107):

items.v: your medical expenses, up to the PIP level you chose
85 percent of lost wages for up to three years, up to the monthly cap DIFS sets each year
replacement services at $20 a day
attendant care

c.v: The PIP level is not the same as your liability limits.

Since July 2, 2020, Michigan drivers choose a PIP medical level for each policy: unlimited, $500,000, $250,000, $50,000 for some Medicaid enrollees, or an opt-out for some Medicare enrollees (MCL 500.3107c). That choice is separate from the $250,000/$500,000 liability limits that protect the other driver. The level on your declarations page decides how much of your medical care no-fault pays.

If you have no policy, a resident relative’s policy pays (MCL 500.3114). If none exists, an occupant claims from the insurer of the vehicle they were in (MCL 500.3114(4)), and then the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan (MCL 500.3172), capped at $250,000 for medical benefits. A pedestrian or cyclist hit by a car, with no household policy, claims through the Assigned Claims Plan (MCL 500.3115).

The insurer must receive written notice within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)). It must pay each bill within 30 days of reasonable proof, or owe 12 percent interest (MCL 500.3142). Providers’ charges are subject to the fee schedule in MCL 500.3157. See our
no-fault insurance claim page
If you had no insurance.

A person who owned a car and was required to insure it, but did not, is generally barred from PIP benefits for their own injuries (MCL 500.3113(b)). A driver who was operating their own uninsured vehicle cannot recover pain-and-suffering damages, whoever was at fault (MCL 500.3135(2)(c)). A passenger or pedestrian who did not own an uninsured car may still be covered through a household policy or the Assigned Claims Plan.
Your claim against the at-fault driver.

For pain and suffering, you need a threshold injury: death, serious impairment of body function, or permanent serious disfigurement (MCL 500.3135(1)). A serious impairment is an objectively manifested impairment of an important body function that affects your general ability to lead your normal life. It does not have to be permanent (MCL 500.3135(5);
McCormick v Carrier
You can also recover economic losses that no-fault does not cover (MCL 500.3135(3)(c)):

items.v: lost wages beyond the three years or above the monthly cap
medical bills above your chosen PIP level

c.v: The suit must be filed within three years (MCL 600.5805(2)). The mini tort claim recovers up to $3,000 in vehicle damage not covered by your policy (MCL 500.3135(3)(e)). If the at-fault driver’s insurer will not pay it, the claim is filed in the 40th District Court.
When the other driver has no insurance, or not enough.
Some drivers carry only the $50,000 opt-down minimum (MCL 500.3009(5)), and some carry nothing.

items.v: your pain-and-suffering claim is worth what that driver can personally pay, unless you carry

faqs.question: A drunk driver leaving a Jefferson Avenue bar hit me. Can I sue the bar?

answer.v: Possibly. A bar or restaurant that served a visibly intoxicated person can be liable for the injuries that person causes. Written notice must reach the bar within 120 days after you hire a lawyer, the drunk driver must be part of the suit, and the suit must be filed within two years. The bar’s receipts and cameras are the evidence, and they disappear quickly.

faqs.question: I was rear-ended at the I-94 exit at 12 Mile. Who pays?

answer.v: Your own no-fault insurer pays your medical bills and lost wages regardless of fault. For pain and suffering, your claim is against the driver who hit you if your injury meets the threshold. A rear-end crash is rarely disputed on fault, but the other driver’s insurer may still argue about how badly you were hurt, so get medical care the same day.

faqs.question: The driver who hit me had no insurance. What now?

answer.v: Your own no-fault insurer, a household member’s insurer, or the Assigned Claims Plan pays your medical bills and lost wages regardless of fault. Your pain-and-suffering claim depends on whether you carry uninsured motorist coverage. If the driver had been drinking, a claim against the bar that served them may also be available.

faqs.question: Is my PIP medical coverage the same as my $250,000 or $500,000 limit?

answer.v: Not necessarily. Your liability limits protect the other driver if you cause a crash. Your PIP medical level is a separate choice on the same policy, and it decides how much of your own medical care no-fault pays. Check your declarations page for both.

faqs.question: How many crashes are there in St. Clair Shores?

answer.v: The State Police recorded 1,356 crashes in St. Clair Shores in 2024. 3 people were killed, 20 were seriously injured, and 365 were injured in all. 454 of the crashes were on I-94, and 55 involved alcohol.

faqs.question: I was hit on my bike on Jefferson. Who pays my medical bills?

answer.v: Your own household’s auto policy pays if you have one. If not, the Assigned Claims Plan pays. Your pain-and-suffering claim is against the driver. The State Police recorded more bicyclist crashes than pedestrian crashes in the city in 2024.

answer.v: Mini tort claims and claims up to $25,000 go to the 40th District Court on Jefferson Avenue. Injury suits over $25,000 go to the Sixteenth Judicial Circuit Court in Mount Clemens.
